title: Chemical and physical observations in Golfo Dulce, an anoxic basin on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica
summary: The foundational hydrographic occupation of Golfo Dulce and the origin of almost every depth figure later repeated in the literature. Richards and colleagues occupied stations from a ship, lowering bottles and reversing thermometers; the basin depth and the existence of a restricting sill enter the record here as by-products of a chemistry cruise, not of a hydrographic survey. Every subsequent Spanish-language description of the gulf's morphology (Quesada-Alpízar & Cortés 2006, Rincón-Alejos & Ballestero 2016) cites this paper for the sill, which means the sill depth in general circulation has a 1971 station-based provenance rather than a surveyed one.
verbatim_finding: Golfo Dulce is an embayment containing small concentrations of hydrogen sulfide near the bottom due to sulfate reduction.
data_availability: No digital data deposit. Station tables and vertical profiles are printed in the paper itself; the depths are point soundings at CTD/bottle stations, not a survey grid.
caveat: A water-chemistry cruise, not a bathymetric survey. The depths reported are whatever the ship's echo sounder read at a handful of station positions; no track lines, no coverage claim, no stated instrument accuracy.

title: Morphology and sediment structures in Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: This is, as far as this harvest can establish, the only dedicated acoustic survey of the Golfo Dulce sea floor ever published. It was run from R/V Victor Hensen during the 1993/1994 Costa Rica expedition and consists of fourteen sediment-echosounder profiles at 18 kHz — a single-beam, sub-bottom-profiling instrument, not a swath system. It resolves the along-track structure of the inner basin (an oriental fault scarp reaching 170 m of relief, two subordinate parallel faults, turbidite channels feeding the flat basin floor) but by construction it produces lines, not area coverage. Any statement about the shape of the inner basin between those fourteen lines is interpolation. This entry is the answer to 'who measured what, when, with what instrument'.
verbatim_finding: Sediment echosounder records (18 KHz) of 14 profiles were made in the fjord-like embayment of Golfo Dulce.
data_availability: None digitally. The echosounder records are reproduced as figures in the article; no soundings, tracks or grids were archived at NCEI, PANGAEA or GMRT under this cruise as far as could be determined. The article PDF is free at the Revista de Biología Tropical archive.
caveat: Fourteen profile lines over a ~680 km² gulf. Single-beam sub-bottom profiler, not multibeam: it images what is under the ship and nothing to either side. Published in a supplement volume with no DOI, which is part of why it is invisible to most bathymetric data discovery.

title: Sedimentation in a tropical fjord: Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: The follow-up to the 1996 echosounder work, and the only published constraint on the sediment fill of the basin. Working from surface sediments and 3.5 m gravity cores, it separates the gulf floor into turbiditic basin deposits and largely undisturbed hemipelagic slope deposits, and shows that the terrigenous supply dominates (>90% non-biogenic). For the bathymetric question this matters twice over: it establishes that the flat inner-basin floor is a depositional surface rather than bedrock, and — via the sub-bottom records — it is the source of the widely repeated figure that soft recent sediment blankets the gulf to 5-10 m thickness outside the sill area.
verbatim_finding: Sedimentation processes in Golfo Dulce, a periodically anoxic fjord-like embayment on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica, have been investigated by analyses of surface sediments and 3.5-m-long sediment cores.
data_availability: Core and surface-sediment analyses are tabulated in the paper. No PANGAEA deposit was found for these cores. Full text behind Springer paywall.
caveat: Cores are 3.5 m long — they sample the top of the fill only. Total sediment thickness in the basin is not constrained by any published seismic reflection line; there is no deep sub-bottom or multichannel seismic profile inside the gulf in the NCEI trackline archive.

title: A physical-oceanographic study of Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: The most-cited modern statement of the gulf's controlling geometry: an inner basin with a flat bottom at 215 m maximum depth, separated from a shallow outer basin by a sill area 20 km inside the entrance whose effective depth is about 60 m. Critically for our purpose, the paper also shows how thin the bathymetric foundation is under numerical work on this gulf: the Princeton Ocean Model implementation runs on a 66 x 48 cell net at 2 x 2 km resolution, and the authors state only that 'the original bottom matrix is smoothed' — they never cite a source or a survey for that bottom matrix. A 2 km grid cannot resolve a sill that the same paper says is the single control on deep-water renewal.
verbatim_finding: The effective sill depth is about 60 m and prevents water in the inner basin from free exchange with the adjacent coastal water masses.
data_availability: CTD sections, drogue tracks and current-meter records are presented as figures; the model bottom topography appears only as a contour figure (Fig. 11). No grid, no soundings and no bathymetric source are released or named.
caveat: The '60 m effective sill' is an oceanographic inference about exchange, not a surveyed minimum depth over the sill — and it conflicts with the '<30 m' sill quoted in the Spanish literature. The provenance of the model bathymetry is undocumented.

title: Los ecosistemas marinos del Pacífico sur de Costa Rica: estado del conocimiento y perspectivas de manejo
summary: The standard Spanish-language review of what is known about the southern Pacific of Costa Rica, and therefore the clearest window on how the gulf's morphological numbers propagate. It fixes the canonical figures — inner basin 215 m maximum, sill 60 m, area ~680 km² — and attributes them to Cortés (1990), Córdoba & Vargas (1996) and Hebbeln et al. (1996), i.e. to reef mapping, a station-based hydrographic study and the fourteen echosounder lines. It also carries the only Spanish-language statement of sediment thickness in the gulf, again sourced from the Victor Hensen echosounder records. Its own conclusion is that circulation and deep-water/soft-sediment characterisation remain unstudied.
verbatim_finding: se caracteriza por poseer una cuenca interna de pendiente pronunciada con una profundidad máxima de 215 m y un umbral poco profundo (60 m) a su entrada
data_availability: Review article; no primary data. Free PDF from the Revista de Biología Tropical supplement archive. Its value here is the citation chain it exposes for each morphological number.
caveat: Secondary source. Every depth in it is inherited; the review adds no new measurement and does not question the age or coverage of the underlying surveys.

title: Hidrografía y plumas estuarinas en Golfo Dulce, Pacífico Sur de Costa Rica
summary: A 33-station CTD campaign (2009-2010) whose introduction is the sharpest available evidence that the sill depth is genuinely unconstrained: it states the sill is shallower than 30 m, citing Richards et al. 1971, while Svendsen et al. 2006 — cited two sentences later in the same paragraph for the tidal range — give about 60 m. Both figures circulate simultaneously in the peer-reviewed Spanish literature on the same gulf. The paper also inherits the 215 m inner-basin / 70 m outer-basin split from Wolff, Hartmann & Koch (1996), a trophic modelling paper, which is a striking provenance for a bathymetric statement.
verbatim_finding: Un umbral o silla con menos de 30m ubicado en su entrada restringe la circulación y hace más lenta la renovación del agua en las capas profundas favoreciendo condiciones anóxicas en el fondo
data_availability: CTD profiles, Secchi and chlorophyll-a measurements at 33 stations, presented as figures and sections; no archived data files. Open-access full text at SciELO Costa Rica and revistas.ucr.ac.cr.
caveat: The two sill depths in circulation (<30 m here, ~60 m in Svendsen et al. 2006) differ by a factor of two and neither traces to a survey line across the sill. The CTD in January 2009 reached only 66 m, so this campaign did not itself sound the deep basin.

title: A fjord-like tropical ecosystem, Pacific coast of Costa Rica: overview of research in Golfo Dulce
summary: A systematic sweep of 123 studies containing Golfo Dulce data, and therefore the best single test of whether a modern survey exists: across the whole corpus the authors identify no bathymetric or seafloor-mapping survey after the 1993/1994 Victor Hensen expedition, and their own list of research priorities asks for basic measurements of exchange over the sill — a question that cannot be answered without knowing the sill's geometry. If a multibeam survey of the inner basin had been published, this review is where it would appear.
verbatim_finding: Golfo Dulce has low oxygen concentrations below 50 m and is frequently anoxic at the 200 m deep basin with occasional formation of H2S.
data_availability: Bibliographic synthesis; the value is the reference list itself, which is complete enough to serve as a negative-evidence check. Open access.
caveat: A literature review, so absence of a survey in it is strong but not conclusive evidence of absence — a purely hydrographic or naval survey might never enter the biological literature this review sampled.

title: A carbonate platform associated with shallow cold methane seeps in Golfo Dulce, Pacific Costa Rica
container: Galaxea, Journal of Coral Reef Studies
summary: Evidence that the gulf floor still yields first discoveries to a diver with a bag: a 100 m² authigenic carbonate platform standing 2 m above the surrounding mud at 10 m depth, emitting >85% methane gas, found in 2012 and reported as the first shallow tropical cold seep known outside hydrothermal settings. A structure of that relief and extent is exactly what a survey-grade echosounder resolves and what a 15 arc-second interpolated grid cannot. Its discovery by chance, seventeen years after the last acoustic survey, is a concrete measure of how much of the sea floor remains uncharacterised.
verbatim_finding: In January 2012, we observed gas emissions from a carbonate platform (ca. 100 m2 in area) formed about 2 m above muddy sediments at 10 m water depth.
data_availability: Photographs, gas chromatography and stable-carbon-isotope values reported in a two-page photogallery note. Free PDF at J-Stage. One position is given: 8.496450°N, 83.262610°W.
caveat: A short note, not a mapping study — a single site, no acoustic survey of the seep field's extent, and no bathymetric data released.

title: IHO/OHI Publication C-55: Status of Hydrographic Surveying and Charting Worldwide
summary: The authoritative international register of how well each coastal state's waters are surveyed, and the single hardest number available for this project. The Costa Rica entry (compilation retrieved 31 July 2026) records that for waters shallower than 200 m only 10% is adequately surveyed and 90% requires re-survey; for waters deeper than 200 m the figures are 5% and 95%. Golfo Dulce, at 215 m maximum and with the whole gulf inside the 200 m contour bar the basin floor, falls in the 90%-requires-re-survey category. The notes add that the top national priority is a modern survey of port approaches — that is, not of a remote fjord basin.
verbatim_finding: Top priority is modern survey of the approaches to all ports.
data_availability: Free 528-page trilingual PDF, one page per state, regenerated on request from the IHO C-55 database; per-country figures are supplied by national authorities via an online form. No machine-readable download of the underlying database is offered publicly.
caveat: The Costa Rica page is flagged '(B)' and its own note states 'Percentages provided by USNOO and subject to concurrence of national authority' — the percentages are a US Naval Oceanographic Office estimate, not a Costa Rican measurement. Costa Rica's own 2024 national report says it has no C-55 update to offer.

title: Informe Nacional para las Comisiones Hidrográficas Regionales — Costa Rica 2024 (MACHC25)
container: 25ª Conferencia de la Comisión Hidrográfica Mesoamericana y del Mar Caribe (MACHC25), Organización Hidrográfica Internacional
summary: Costa Rica's own account, in Spanish, of its hydrographic capacity — and the reason no modern survey of Golfo Dulce exists. The state has no dedicated hydrographic office: soundings are done piecemeal by the MOPT's Proceso de Hidrografía y Topografía for port works and siltation control, and by IMARES-UCR. The report states plainly that there are no vessels for large-scale bathymetry, no specialised equipment for it, no capacity for satellite-derived or crowdsourced bathymetry, no recent updates to national paper charts, and no update to submit to IHO C-55. A National Hydrographic Committee was still being formed in 2024. This is the institutional explanation for the 90%-unsurveyed figure.
verbatim_finding: No se cuenta con buques específicos para llevar a cabo batimetrías a gran escala.
data_availability: Lists topo-bathymetric surveys carried out by PHT-DOMP-MOPT from 2021 onward (an activity recorded since 1973); all are port-works and siltation surveys, none in Golfo Dulce. No data are published or distributed. Free PDF on the IHO server.
caveat: The report carries no named author; it is a state submission to a regional IHO commission. Its survey list covers 2021 onward only, so it cannot by itself rule out an older national survey of the gulf.

title: NGA Nautical Chart 21562: Golfo Dulce
summary: The only nautical chart dedicated to Golfo Dulce, and a direct measure of the charting vintage. Edition 14 is dated 14 February 1998 at a scale of 1:72,990, last corrected by Notice to Mariners 18 of 1998 — nearly three decades stale. At that scale one millimetre on the paper is 73 m on the water, so the chart cannot represent basin-floor structure at all; it is a navigational document showing enough soundings to keep a hull off the bottom. NGA has since cancelled the chart and no longer serves it for viewing, meaning the best-scale published chart of the gulf is both obsolete and withdrawn.
verbatim_finding: Scale: 72990 Actual Chart Size: 27.2" x 33.1" Paper Size: 36.0" x 35.0" Edition #: 14 Edition Date: 1998-02-14 NTM Notice/Date: 199818 None
data_availability: Print-on-demand paper only via commercial agents; NGA no longer serves the raster image ('charts in this region cannot be viewed'). No digital soundings, no ENC, no source-survey diagram accessible.
caveat: Metadata retrieved from a commercial print agent rather than from NGA directly, because NGA has cancelled and withdrawn the chart. The chart's own source-survey diagram — which would date the underlying soundings — could not be inspected.

title: ADMIRALTY Chart 2493: Ports on the Pacific Coast of Costa Rica and Panama
summary: The British Admiralty's only coverage of the gulf, and it is coarser than the American one: Golfo Dulce appears as panel A of a three-panel plans chart at 1:100,000, sharing the sheet with Puerto Golfito (1:25,000) and two Panamanian ports. That the UKHO devotes a single 1:100,000 inset to a 50 km fjord with a 215 m anoxic basin — while giving four times that scale to the pier at Golfito — shows where hydrographic effort has historically gone: to berths and approaches, not to the basin. There is no larger-scale Admiralty coverage of the gulf interior.
verbatim_finding: A Costa Rica, Golfo Dulce 1:100,000 B Costa Rica, Puerto Golfito 1:25,000 C Panama, Puerto Armuelles and Charco Azul 1:25,000
data_availability: Commercial paper chart and ENC only; soundings are not distributed as data. Corrected to the latest Notices to Mariners by the agent at time of sale.
caveat: Edition date could not be established from an authoritative UKHO source without purchase, so the year is recorded as null rather than guessed. The panel scales are confirmed; the vintage of the underlying survey is not.

title: Carta Esferica desde el Golfo Dulce en la Costa Rica hasa Sn. Blas en la Nueva Galicia
summary: The deepest layer of the charting record for this coast, and it starts at Golfo Dulce: the Spanish Hydrographic Office's 1822 sheet takes the gulf as its southern limit and runs north to San Blas at 1:2,800,000, built on the 1789-1794 Malaspina expedition. It establishes that the gulf entered European hydrography as an endpoint on a passage chart rather than as a place to be surveyed, and that the first systematic soundings of this coast were made under sail more than two centuries ago. At that scale the whole gulf is a few millimetres wide; it fixes the coastline, not the sea floor.
verbatim_finding: Representing the most advanced data available to the Spanish Admiralty at the time, this 1822 Direccion Hidrografía nautical chart or maritime map details the Pacific coast of Central America from southern Mexico and Guatemala to Costa Rica.
data_availability: Original sheet held privately (this copy sold); a high-resolution TIFF scan is offered for purchase by the dealer. No soundings in digital form.
caveat: Retrieved from an antiquarian map dealer, so the descriptive text quoted is the dealer's, not the chart's. Title and 1:2,800,000 scale are read off the sheet itself in the listing. The chart is included as evidence of charting lineage, not as a source of depths.

title: GEBCO_2026 Grid: General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans gridded bathymetry data
authors: General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans
container: General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans / British Oceanographic Data Centre
summary: The global grid that everything else in this gulf ultimately rests on, including GMRT's fill layer. Its cell size is 15 arc-seconds — roughly 460 m of longitude at 8.5°N — so a single GEBCO cell spans about a fifth of the width of the Golfo Dulce sill. GEBCO ships a companion Type Identifier (TID) grid precisely because most cells are not measured: the TID codes distinguish direct soundings from predicted, interpolated and pre-generated values. Anyone quoting a Golfo Dulce depth from GEBCO is quoting an interpolation unless the TID for that cell says otherwise, and the coverage analysis for this gulf indicates it very rarely does.
verbatim_finding: a global terrain model for ocean and land, providing elevation data, in meters, on a 15 arc-second interval grid
data_availability: Free download as netCDF, GeoTIFF, Esri ASCII and data GeoTIFF, globally or by user-defined area, plus the separate TID grid identifying each cell's source type. Current release GEBCO_2026, published 23 April 2026, DOI 10.5285/4f68d5c7-45eb-f999-e063-7086abc036fa (DataCite, resolvable at doi.org).
caveat: The DataCite DOI is recorded in the text rather than the doi field because it is not a Crossref record. 15 arc-seconds is a grid spacing, not a resolution claim: in a gulf this size the grid is finer than the data behind it.

title: Global Multi-Resolution Topography (GMRT) Synthesis, version 4.5.0
authors: Marine Geoscience Data System, Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory
summary: The best-available open bathymetric compilation for the gulf, and the one whose own documentation explains why it is thin here. GMRT curates cleaned ship multibeam at ~120 m and blends it over a base of GEBCO 2026 at 15 arc-seconds; a mask layer marks where the high-resolution data actually contribute. Version 4.5.0 (June 2026) holds 1,644 swath surveys covering 12.41% of the global ocean. Golfo Dulce is in the other 87.6%: a GMRT GridServer request over the gulf returns the same grid at resolution=max, high and med, which is the signature of a request being served from the interpolated base rather than from swath data.
verbatim_finding: The current version (GMRT v4.5.0) was released in June 2026 and includes swath data from 1,644 surveys covering 44,896,399 square kilometers or 12.41% of the global ocean.
data_availability: Open web services: GridServer (Esri ASCII, netCDF, GeoTIFF), MaskServer, PointServer, profiles, WMS, and GeoMapApp. Retrieved directly for the gulf on 31 July 2026: GridServer over 8.35-8.80°N, 83.10-83.55°W returned an 822 x 821 grid at 5.4931640625e-04° cells (~61 m), with the topo-mask layer showing land masking only.
caveat: GMRT will resample its base layer to whatever cell size you request, so a ~61 m output grid over Golfo Dulce is not evidence of ~61 m data. Independent analysis of the returned grid for this project found only 2.6% of the gulf resting on real soundings, 0.0-0.1% above 150 m depth, plus artefact clusters reaching -2058 m in a basin the literature puts a little over 200 m deep.

title: Global Multi-Resolution Topography synthesis
summary: The methods paper behind GMRT, and the citation that GMRT's own documentation directs users to. It sets out the multi-resolution tiling scheme that preserves the native resolution of swath sonar where it exists and degrades gracefully to compiled global grids where it does not — the mechanism that makes a place like Golfo Dulce look mapped when zoomed out and dissolve into interpolation when zoomed in. Its opening sentence is the honest global statement of the problem this project is about.
verbatim_finding: Seafloor bathymetric data acquired with modern swath echo sounders provide coverage for only a small fraction of the global seabed yet are of high value for studies of the dynamic processes of seafloor volcanism, tectonics, mass wasting, and sediment transport
data_availability: Describes the web services and clients through which the synthesis is distributed; the compilation itself is at marine-geo.org/portals/gmrt. Open access at AGU.
caveat: 2009 methods paper; the synthesis has advanced to v4.5.0 since, so version-specific numbers must come from the GMRT site rather than from here.

title: Global Bathymetry and Topography at 15 Arc Sec: SRTM15+
summary: The reference for what a 15 arc-second global grid actually is where no ship has been: depths predicted from satellite-altimeter gravity, not measured. It quantifies both the coverage and the penalty — only 10.84% of the ocean floor is constrained by shipboard soundings at 15 arc-second resolution, and altimetry-constrained cells carry uncertainties of ±150 to ±180 m. For a basin whose entire depth range is about 215 m, an altimetric prediction with ±180 m uncertainty near the coast carries no information at all. This is the quantitative basis for saying that a GEBCO or GMRT depth in Golfo Dulce is not a measurement.
verbatim_finding: Bathymetric grid cells constrained by satellite altimetry have estimated uncertainties of ±150 m in the deep oceans and ±180 m between coastlines and the continental rise.
data_availability: SRTM15+ grid distributed openly by Scripps Institution of Oceanography (topex.ucsd.edu) as netCDF; the paper documents the sounding and altimetry inputs. Open access.
caveat: Altimetric prediction is designed for the deep ocean; inside a 10-15 km wide gulf the gravity signal is dominated by the surrounding land and the method is not applicable, which the ±180 m near-coast figure understates rather than captures.

title: NCEI Multibeam Bathymetry Database and IHO Data Centre for Digital Bathymetry (Seafloor Mapping)
authors: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
IHO Data Centre for Digital Bathymetry
container: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
summary: The world's public archive of ship multibeam, and the decisive negative result for this topic. Querying its survey-footprint service directly on 31 July 2026 for the inner basin (83.45-83.15°W, 8.55-8.75°N) returns zero surveys. Widening to the whole gulf and its mouth returns exactly three, all deep-ocean transits that pass offshore and never enter the gulf: ARIA02WT (R/V Thomas Washington, 1982, SeaBeam), NEMO03MV (R/V Melville, 2000, SeaBeam 2000) and DANA02RR (R/V Roger Revelle, 2003, Simrad EM120). Checking their track coordinates confirms none has a single vertex inside the gulf. No multibeam echosounder has ever been run inside Golfo Dulce and archived publicly.
verbatim_finding: NCEI and the IHO Data Center for Digital Bathymetry (DCDB) archive and share depth data acquired by hydrographic, oceanographic, and industry vessels and platforms during surveys or while on passage.
data_availability: Free and unrestricted. Queried via the ArcGIS REST endpoint gis.ngdc.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/web_mercator/multibeam_dynamic/MapServer/0/query with an esriGeometryEnvelope in EPSG:4326; results reproducible. Raw sonar files and derived grids are downloadable per survey.
caveat: Absence from NCEI is not absolute absence: a national, naval or commercial survey held privately would not appear. But NCEI is the IHO's designated global data centre, so anything intended for public or charting use should be here.

title: NCEI Marine Trackline Geophysical Data (single-beam bathymetry, sub-bottom and seismic)
authors: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
container: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
summary: The companion archive that closes off the pre-multibeam era, covering single-beam bathymetry, sub-bottom profiles and seismic reflection from 1939 to the present with worldwide coverage. Queried on 31 July 2026, the inner-basin envelope returns zero bathymetry tracks and zero multichannel seismic lines. Widening to the whole gulf returns three Scripps deep-ocean transits — PAPA02BD (R/V Spencer F. Baird, 1965), ARIA02WT (1982) and NEMO03MV (2000) — whose bounding boxes span thousands of kilometres of open Pacific. So there is no archived single-beam sounding line inside Golfo Dulce either, and no seismic profile from which sediment thickness or basement depth could be read.
verbatim_finding: NCEI's Marine Trackline Geophysical database provides single-beam bathymetry, subbottom profiles, magnetic, gravity, side-scan sonar and historic seismic reflection and refraction data collected during marine cruises from 1939–present.
data_availability: Free; exportable in MGD77T. Queried via gis.ngdc.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/web_mercator/trackline_combined_dynamic/MapServer layers 1 (Bathymetry) and 4 (Multi-Channel Seismics) with the same envelopes as the multibeam query.
caveat: Coverage is strongest for US and allied academic cruises; small-boat or national surveys never submitted to NCEI are invisible to this query. The Victor Hensen 1993/94 echosounder lines of Hebbeln et al. are a case in point — they exist in print but not in this archive.

title: Allen Coral Atlas satellite-derived bathymetry and habitat mapping methods
authors: Arizona State University Center for Global Discovery and Conservation Science
summary: The realistic ceiling on satellite-derived bathymetry for this gulf, and a useful check on optimism about filling the gap from space. The Atlas produces 10 m bathymetry from Sentinel-2 surface reflectance, using a 12-month median composite chosen for minimal cloud and turbid water, with geomorphic mapping to about 15 m depth and benthic mapping to about 10 m. Golfo Dulce receives more than 4.5 m of rain a year through four rivers and carries surface plumes that drop salinity below 30 over a third of its area, so the optically shallow window the method needs is exactly what the gulf lacks. Satellite methods can address the reef margins; they cannot see the 215 m basin.
verbatim_finding: The bathymetry maps are created at a resolution of 10 m using the Google Earth Engine (GEE) Sentinel-2 surface reflectance dataset.
data_availability: Bathymetry, geomorphic and benthic layers downloadable as GeoTIFF (16-bit integer, depth in centimetres) after free registration, for mapped coral reef areas between roughly 30°N and 30°S.
caveat: Methods page is undated, so year is recorded as null. Coverage of the Golfo Dulce margins specifically was not verified layer-by-layer in this harvest; the entry documents the method's depth and turbidity limits, which is the point that matters here.
